title: "Grants as code: compiled budgets, funder views, and machine-checkable applications"
author:
  - name: Max Ghenis
    affiliations: [PolicyEngine, The Axiom Foundation]
date: 2026-08-15
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
abstract: >
  Grant applications are often assembled by hand from three kinds of
  material: the work an organization intends to do, the cost of the people
  and systems that do it, and the rules of the funder's form. We describe a
  pipeline that represents each as data — a priced menu of work items with a
  required completion-evidence field; modeled guaranteed employer costs
  derived from encoded tax rules and a stated retirement-cap assumption,
  with optional benchmark provenance; funder proposals as selections over
  the shared menu, with co-funding fractions that support a pre-award
  over-allocation check within the modeled portfolio; and versioned funder
  packs that validate and assemble the application in continuous
  integration. A targeted scan across six tool lanes plus an adjacent-fields
  pass assesses prior art. In this US-centric, English-language scan, novel
  means no prior art found, not proven absent. The pre-award
  cross-application gate is novel as a machine check; related federal
  anti-overlap and anti-double-charge principles are longstanding.
  Funder-as-view is novel as a mechanism: named ancestors copy estimates or
  text, or share organizational profiles, but do not constrain proposals as
  fractional views over a priced substrate. The proposed funder-facing
  configurator is novel, with the thinnest neighbor set of the six claims,
  but is not implemented in 0.3 and its adoption is untested. Budget
  compilation and rule-derived rates are partially anticipated — rate-table
  engines and payroll calculators exist — and survive only in their precise
  forms. Validation already runs at scale in NIH ASSIST; the contribution
  here is open, versioned, applicant-controlled, repo-resident,
  funder-portable rule packs — a domain transfer of the compliance-as-code
  pattern. The budget engine and schemas are implemented on a review branch
  for the companion grantkit 0.3 release; grantkit 0.2.x is available on PyPI
  today under the MIT license. The reference rates provider remains private,
  with public release pending.

# The claims {#sec-claims}

The paper stands or falls on six claims. Each was tested adversarially
against six tool lanes plus an adjacent-fields pass: a targeted scan was
instructed to find prior art against each claim, and its verdicts appear in
brackets after each claim, argued in full in @sec-landscape.

**C1 — Budgets as compiled artifacts.** A grant budget should be the output
of a pure function over (menu items, rates, selection), reproducible in CI,
not a spreadsheet edited toward a total. Changing a rate or a selection
regenerates the compiled Markdown and JSON artifacts identically; proposal
documents, funder decks, and internal planning pages can consume those
artifacts. [Verdict: partial
prior art. Rate-table budget engines and structured cost buildup exist,
closed or — where once open — frozen since 2017. We concede the loose form,
"computing budgets from data"; the claim survives only as stated: pure
function, work-item menu, reproducible in CI.]

**C2 — The pre-award over-allocation gate.** When proposals are selections
with per-item co-funding fractions, "no item is more than 100% funded across
simultaneous applications" becomes a machine-checked portfolio rule when a
selection enters live status. In a pre-submission workflow, an organization
marks a proposal live before sending it. Institutional effort-reporting
systems used to document personnel charges under 2 CFR 200.430 are related,
retrospective controls, not the same per-item rule. [Verdict: novel as a
machine check. The underlying anti-overlap and anti-double-charge principles
are old federal policy; the per-item planning rule is this system's
operationalization, and the novelty claim is enforcement timing plus
automation.]

**C3 — Rule-derived personnel rates.** Modeled guaranteed employer costs
computed from encoded rules — employer payroll taxes by jurisdiction and a
stated employer-contribution ceiling constructed from IRS §415(c) and
§402(g) limits — rather than a pooled fringe multiplier, with optional market
benchmarks (BLS OEWS, sourced percentiles) attached per role. The budget's
comp-justification appendix becomes a generated artifact. [Verdict:
partial prior art. The computation exists in payroll-tax calculators; the
benchmarks exist as data products. We concede the loose
form, "computing employer burden from rules"; what was not found is the
composition — rule-derived employer costs in a pre-award rate object capable
of carrying optional benchmark provenance inside a budget compilation.]

**C4 — Funder-as-view.** One organizational substrate (the menu), many
proposals as selections over it. The org maintains its work-item database
once; each funder sees a view: selected items, fractions, an org-base
allocation, a window. Views make co-funding legible instead of narrative.
[Verdict: novel as a mechanism. The ancestors reuse estimates or text by
copying forward, share organizational profiles, standardize forms, or braid
funding manually; none constrains N live proposals as fractional views over
one priced substrate.]

**C5 — Funder packs: the application as a checked build.** Funder form rules
— section structure, word/character/page limits, budget caps, required
attachments, placeholder gates — as versioned code; the application repo
builds in CI to a status artifact and an assembled document. (Shipped in
grantkit 0.2.x; @sec-pipeline.) [Verdict: the core exists at scale, closed —
NIH ASSIST validates against encoded business rules and reports itemized
errors and warnings. What remains, and what we claim, is the open,
versioned, applicant-controlled, locally runnable, funder-portable packaging
with a repo-resident status artifact — the compliance-as-code pattern carried
into a new domain.]

**C6 — The configurator.** Because budgets compile (C1), we propose a
funder-facing surface: presets and toggles over the same menu and rates the
organization runs on, with attempted configurations compiled and checked by
the existing gates. This would make scenario pressure-testing interactive
rather than a static appendix. [Verdict: novel, with the thinnest neighbor
set of the six. The interface is not implemented in 0.3 and funder adoption
is untested; @sec-case reports pressure-testing of the underlying model, not
use of a configurator.]

The through-line — and the paper's one-sentence thesis: **when grant inputs
become versioned data processed by deterministic builds and explicit checks,
the pipeline can acquire software-pipeline properties: reproducibility,
textual diffs, and invariants checked before submission rather than only
reviewed after award.**

# Landscape {#sec-landscape}

We conducted an August 2026 sweep (2026-08-14/15) across six tool lanes plus
an adjacent-fields pass — vendor documentation, help centers, and federal
guidance, discounting marketing claims where the docs said less — with an
adversarial brief: find prior art against each claim. This was a targeted web
and product scan, not a systematic literature review. One caveat governs
everything that follows: the sweep was US-centric and English-language, so a
verdict of *novel* means no prior art found, not proven absent.

## Applicant-side writing tools

Does any grant-writing tool derive budgets from structured work-item data?
The finding: they draft narrative text and track awards; none compiles a
budget from a work-item substrate. The closest thing to budget generation in
this lane is a language model writing a budget-shaped table as prose.

[Instrumentl](https://www.instrumentl.com/product-overview) pairs grant
discovery with tracking and post-award management; its budget feature,
[Budget Spenddown Tracking](https://www.instrumentl.com/blog/grant-spenddown-tracking),
tracks expenses against an award budget in real time, with spending goals
by category and expense uploads from accounting — post-award and
expense-side (the feature's help article is login-gated; we describe what
the public blog post documents). [Grantable](https://grantable.co/) runs
[AI drafting over a content library](https://www.grantable.co/features/ai-grant-writing-assistant)
— write once, reuse across proposals — a narrative cousin of C4's substrate,
with no budget model, no fractions, no checks.
[Granted AI](https://grantedai.com/features) matches funders from
990-derived profiles, analyzes RFPs, drafts section by section, and
simulates a six-reviewer committee; budget appears only as interview
questions that ground the narrative, and the committee is stochastic
critique, not machine-checkable validation. FreeWill's
[Grant Assistant](https://www.nonprofits.freewill.com/products/grant-assistant)
is the lane's nearest neighbor to C5: its
[Respond tool](https://www.grantassistant.ai/respond) derives a matrix of the
funding opportunity's requirements and scans the draft to confirm each
requirement is addressed, helping applicants "catch overlooked errors before
you submit" — but the matrix is model-generated per proposal, not a
versioned, citable rule pack, and the check is advisory prose, not a
deterministic exit code.
[Streamline](https://streamlineclimate.com/solutions/startup) runs an AI
grant and RFP pipeline for climate applicants — opportunity search,
solicitation summarization, drafting, reuse — narrative only.
[Grantboost](https://www.grantboost.io/nonprofits/) generates proposals from
a survey and honors per-section word and character limits: the germ of a
funder rule, with no encoded pack, no lint, no artifact. Submittable's
applicant side fills funder-built web forms behind
[eligibility screeners](https://submittable.help/en/articles/3872413-eligibility-forms)
with required-field and type validation — machine gating exists, but the
rules live inside the funder's portal, invisible and unversioned from the
applicant's side. [OpenGrants](https://opengrants.io/for-grant-seekers/),
despite the name, is open *data access* — a search engine over 70k+
listings, a grant-writer marketplace, and a REST API — not open-source
tooling. And a genre of free prompt tools, represented by LogicBalls'
[AI grant budget template](https://logicballs.com/tools/grant-budget-template),
has a model write the budget table from a project description: C1's contrast
in its purest form, a budget as generated text with no documented
reproducibility mechanism.

The lane kills nothing. Its strongest neighbor is Grant Assistant's
requirements matrix — C5-adjacent and non-deterministic.

## Funder-side grants management

Does any grants management system expose applicant-controlled budget
composition, or validation rules the applicant can inspect and run locally?
The products reviewed validate form fields and workflow state; none was found
to see inside the applicant's cost model or check allocation across a
portfolio of applications to other funders.

[Fluxx Grantmaker](https://www.fluxx.io/products/grantmaker-fluxx-grants-management-software)
gives funders configurable forms and workflows, a grantee portal, budget and
finance tracking of awards, and automated validation steps — required
fields, data standardization — all portal-side and per-form, with budgets as
attachments and line tables.
[Foundant GLM](https://www.foundant.com/products/grant-management-software-for-foundations/)
runs application through review, payment, and follow-up for small and
mid-size foundations, with a branching form builder and budgets tracked as
program-level allocations drawn down by payments.
[Submittable's funder side](https://www.submittable.com/features/online-forms)
builds forms, gates eligibility, stages review, and validates applicant data
against third-party databases.
[SmartSimple Cloud](https://www.smartsimple.com/solution/grants-management-tracking-software)
adds eligibility quizzes, IRS and watchlist vetting, and a Budget Manager
whose business rules drive funder-side budget and payment schedules — rules
that govern the funder's payments, not the applicant's budget composition.
Salesforce grantmaking spans the free, open-source
[Outbound Funds Module](https://appexchange.salesforce.com/appxListingDetail?listingId=a0N3A00000G5vDxUAJ)
— funding programs, requests, disbursements, expenditures — and the
commercial Nonprofit Cloud for Grantmaking; notable as the lane's one
open-source artifact, it models money movement, not application content or
budget derivation.
[Blackbaud Grantmaking](https://webfiles-sc1.blackbaud.com/files/support/helpfiles/grantmaking/content/budget-phase1.html)
manages funder budget hierarchies — categories, reserve funds, line items —
with payment appropriation controls and, since 2024, an applicant portal
with an AI form builder; the budget machinery is entirely funder-internal.
[WizeHive Zengine](https://softwareconnect.com/reviews/wizehive-zengine/) is
a flexible form, review, and workflow builder for grants, scholarships, and
awards. [AmpliFund](https://www.amplifund.com/features/) comes closest to
budget mechanics, tracking budgets, indirect costs, and staff hours through
the award lifecycle for governments that receive and pass through funds —
still award tracking, not proposal compilation.

The lane sharpens C5 rather than killing it: machine validation of
applications is common inside closed hosted systems, so the novelty left is
applicant-controlled, local, versioned, open, funder-portable rule packs with
a repo-resident status artifact.

## Nonprofit budgeting and finance

Does anything gate multi-funder allocation before award? Multi-funder
allocation turns out to be a solved *post-award accounting* problem and a
supported *budget-planning* feature; nothing gates allocation across
simultaneous, not-yet-awarded proposals.

[Sage Intacct's grants tracking and billing](https://www.sage.com/en-us/sage-business-cloud/intacct/product-capabilities/extended-capabilities/grants-tracking-billing/)
associates entries with grants at transaction entry, bills indirect costs
at negotiated, specific, or markup rates, and tracks employee effort per
grant from integrated timekeeping data. This is one post-award control
against duplicate charging: transaction by transaction, through bookkeeping
discipline. [Martus](https://www.martussolutions.com/capabilities/personnel) is the
lane's nearest neighbor to C2 and C4: its personnel budgeting supports an
employee funded by multiple grants, allocated by hours, amount, or
percentage, by month or year. A person split across grants by percentage is
structurally analogous to a co-funding fraction — but Martus is an internal
planning worksheet for known or expected funding: no notion of simultaneous
pending applications, no constraint that fractions across open proposals sum
to at most one, no machine gate, no artifact a funder sees.
[Limelight](https://www.golimelight.com/industries/non-profit) has the same
shape — nonprofit FP&A templates for grants, funds, programs, and workforce
planning. On the free end, Propel Nonprofits'
[True Program Costs template](https://propelnonprofits.org/resources/true-program-costs-program-budget-and-allocation-template-and-resource/)
is an example of budget-from-structure: a spreadsheet with formulas. Its
arithmetic is computed and can be audited; the contrast here is the lack of a
textual schema, headless CI build, and portfolio-wide gate outside the
workbook. The Wallace Foundation's
[StrongNonprofits toolkit](https://wallacefoundation.org/toolkit/strongnonprofits-toolkit?s=budgeting)
ships a
[Program-Based Budget Builder](https://wallacefoundation.org/sites/default/files/2023-10/program-based-budget-builder-overview.pdf)
that allocates personnel and shared costs to programs, and an
out-of-school-time cost calculator that "works like a mortgage calculator" —
a genuine closed-form cost model exposed to planners, and so a C6 ancestor,
but built on generic benchmarks rather than the org's own live model, and
not aimed at funder diligence. The direct incumbent for C3 remains the pooled
fringe-rate practice documented in the Kuali and Cayuse systems below;
indirect-cost recovery is a different cost concept, not a substitute for
employer payroll and retirement costs. And the
[fund-accounting validation genre](https://www.criadv.com/insight/managing-restricted-funds/)
prevents charging the wrong fund and distributes expenses across funds on
entry: the don't-bill-twice invariant, in production software, post-award
and expense-by-expense.

The lane establishes that percentage allocation exists in planning tools
(Martus) and controls against duplicate charging exist in accounting tools
(Intacct et al.) — both outside the pre-award window and neither identical to
the per-work-item gate proposed here.

## Federal compliance machinery

What exists for cross-application allocation checking, and is any of it
pre-award and automatic? Related rules — no more than 100% personnel
commitment and no duplicate charging — are old and explicit. We found human
review at each pre-award point. The paper's per-work-item allocation rule is
a stricter organizational planning control, not a claim that federal policy
already defines the identical object. Budget arithmetic and form validation,
by contrast, are heavily automated inside closed systems.

Effort certification is the incumbent answer to cross-source personnel
allocation.
[Huron ECC](https://www.huronconsultinggroup.com/-/media/Resource-Media-Content/Education/research-suite/Huron-Research-Suite-Employee-Compensation-Compliance.pdf),
née ecrt, supports university compliance with 2 CFR 200.430: it
[generates effort and payroll statements](https://finance.uw.edu/pafc/effort-reporting/ecc-system/ecc-overview)
that principal investigators certify *after the fact*, as traditional effort
reporting or project-based payroll confirmation.
[Maximus ERS](https://maximus.com/specialized-markets/higher-ed/effort-reporting-system-and-services)
is the same category — web-based certification with escalation workflows
for delinquent forms. Both are strong evidence *for* C2's novelty: the
incumbent solution is post-award attestation, workflow-managed but
substantively human.

The policy layer for C2 is current-and-pending support. NIH's
[Grants Policy Statement §2.5.1](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/policy/nihgps/HTML5/section_2/2.5.1_just-in-time_procedures.htm)
does not permit commitment overlap — more than 100% or twelve person-months
across all support — and resolves it "with the applicant and the PD/PI at
the time of award": staff read just-in-time submissions and negotiate
([UW–Madison's summary](https://rsp.wisc.edu/other-support-information.cfm)).
University pre-award offices review the forms so listed effort sums
correctly (e.g.,
[Tufts OVPR guidance](https://viceprovost.tufts.edu/policies-forms-guides/current-and-pending-other-support-proposals-and-awards)).
[NSF's current-and-pending FAQ](https://www.nsf.gov/funding/senior-personnel-documents/faq/current-pending)
describes using the data to "assess the capacity of the individual" and
potential "overlap/duplication," with no automated summation documented.
We found no agency system that automatically sums commitments across
applications; the guidance reviewed describes staff review. This is the
closest related practice to C2 found in the scan: personnel-overlap review is
standard, while the exact per-work-item machine gate is absent.

[NIH ASSIST and the eRA validations](https://www.era.nih.gov/about-era/other-services/validations)
are the strongest single prior art against C5. Applications are validated
against "many of NIH and Grants.gov's business rules" before submission;
applications with errors are stopped from submission, warnings do not
block; failures produce an
[itemized errors-and-warnings results page](https://www.era.nih.gov/erahelp/assist/Content/ASSIST_Help_Topics/5_Preview_Print_Submit/Submit_Validated_Application.htm).
Free to applicants, closed system. What it is not: open,
applicant-controlled, locally runnable, versioned by the applicant, or
portable — the rules are opaque implementation, the artifact is a transient
results page, and coverage is federal NIH-family forms.

[Grants.gov](https://www.grants.gov/applicants/encountering-error-messages.html)
rejects applications at submission for schema and format problems — its
public error documentation is a troubleshooting list of submission-time
technical errors ("Mandatory Forms Not Found") rather than a validation
specification, and documents no pre-submission cross-form checks. Its
[system-to-system pages](https://www.grants.gov/system-to-system/grantor-system-to-system/schemas)
publish versioned XML schemas for opportunity and application handling
(e.g., GrantsCommonTypes-V1.0, GrantsCommonElements-V1.0,
ApplicantCommonElements-V1.0, GrantsFundingSynopsis-V2.0); the
[forms repository](https://grants.gov/forms/forms-repository/sf-424-family)
serves the SF-424 family as sample PDFs marked not submittable, and we did
not confirm per-form XSDs on the public pages. Partial prior art for C5's
"form rules as code": federal system-to-system interchange is literally
versioned schema, but the public pages document format enforcement rather
than encoded business rules or caps, the validator is a hosted black box,
and nothing lands in the applicant's repo.

[Cayuse 424](https://support.cayuse.com/hc/en-us/articles/115013731528)
builds system-to-system proposals with a running errors-warnings-info list
replicating Grants.gov and agency validations, and
[auto-calculates budgets](https://support.cayuse.com/hc/en-us/articles/115013737108-Adding-Fringe-Rates-and-Benefits-in-Proposals-S2S)
from institutional profiles — fringe rate tables, set as percentages or
per-person dollar amounts, with escalation and indirect-cost rates
configured as separate institutional settings. That is prior art
against C5 (live validation with severity levels) and against C1's weak form
(budgets computed from structured inputs and rate tables). What is missing
for C1 proper: the inputs are cost categories and rates, not a work-item
menu; the computation is interactive and stateful, not a pure function; and
the reviewed documentation describes no external reproducibility path.
[Kuali Research's budget engine](https://kuali-research.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/115010656047-Proposal-Budget-Budget-Engine-Calculations)
is the same shape — institutional rate tables driving automatic calculation
"on a precise daily calculation," with cost share and unrecovered F&A — and
the sharpest C3 contrast in the wild: fringe is *defined* as salary times a
configured rate; in the grant tooling reviewed, none we found computes it
from statute. Kuali is also not simply
closed: the engine descends from MIT's Coeus through Kuali Coeus, community
source under the Educational Community License from 2006, spun off
for-profit in 2014; the open-source ancestor
([github.com/kuali/kc](https://github.com/kuali/kc), AGPL-3.0) remains
public but frozen since January 2017, and the current commercial engine is
closed.

The closest pre-award multi-funder allocation practice found in this scan is
the Advance Planning Document regime in state health and human services
systems.
[45 CFR 95.610](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/95.610) defines the
APD's contents — a proposed budget and "an estimate of the prospective cost
allocation/distribution to the various State and Federal funding sources" —
and [§95.611](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/95.611) requires
approval *before* acquisition;
[CMS](https://www.medicaid.gov/federal-policy-guidance/downloads/faq061319.pdf)
and [ACF](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ocse/apd_guide_2.pdf)
fund at enhanced matching rates (90/75/50) and publish cost-allocation
methodology toolkits, and multi-program APDs cover systems funded by several
federal programs at once. Conceptually this is C2 plus C4 — one system,
several funders, declared shares, approval before spend. The implementation
is narrative documents, spreadsheet methodologies, and human federal
reviewers: no machine check, no code, no reproducibility. We cite it as the
manual ancestor.

Finally, [SF-424A](https://grants.gov/forms/forms-repository/sf-424-family)
itself — the government-wide budget form, with Section A and B matrices by
object class and funding source and totals that must reconcile, its tooling
a fillable PDF plus the validators above — is the C1 contrast in one object:
the canonical grant budget is a *form*, downstream of whatever spreadsheet
produced the numbers, and provenance ends at data entry.

The lane wounds C5 (validation with status reporting exists at scale,
closed) and C1's weak form (rate-table budget engines exist, closed); it
strengthens C2 and supplies C4's manual ancestor.

## Docs-as-code and policy-as-code

Who already owns the pattern — documents plus rules plus CI plus status
artifacts — and has anyone pointed it at grants? The pattern is mature in
adjacent domains. The scan found no tool, paper, or product styled "grants as
code" or "CI for grants" for grant applications (results were license and
crypto noise).

The nearest live practice is git-native grant programs: the
[Web3 Foundation Grants-Program](https://github.com/w3f/Grants-Program) and
[gno.land grants](https://github.com/gnolang/grants) take
applications as markdown files submitted by pull request and reviewed
in-repo — real prior art for *proposals in git with PR review*, but the
artifact is narrative-only: no budget model, no funder rule packs, no
machine validation of content documented.

[OSCAL and compliance-trestle](https://github.com/oscal-compass/compliance-trestle)
are the strongest pattern-level prior art for C5: NIST schemas plus an
Apache-2.0 CLI under which security compliance documents — SSPs, catalogs —
are authored as markdown and JSON in git, validated and assembled by a tool
"designed to operate as a CICD pipeline running on top of compliance
artifacts" ([oscal.io/tools](https://oscal.io/tools/)). C5's residual
novelty is domain transfer — funder packs, budget caps, submission formats —
not the pattern. [Vale](https://vale.sh/) lints prose against YAML rule
packages in CI, used by the Grafana, Datadog, and Elastic docs teams;
grantkit's `check` is Vale-shaped with funder semantics — limits, required
sections, citations, budget caps.
[docassemble](https://docassemble.org/) (MIT license) assembles legal
documents from structured data through guided interviews in YAML, Python,
and Markdown, and the Suffolk LIT Lab's Assembly Line builds court forms on
it — documents-compiled-from-data is established in legal aid, without
budgets or funder rules.
[Catala](https://www.inria.fr/en/catala-software-dgfip-cnaf) transcribes
statutes into a verified DSL used with the French tax and benefits
administrations, and the
[Accord Project](https://docs.accordproject.org/docs/accordproject-slc.html)
makes contracts computable — together legitimizing C3's premise that
statute-to-code is a proven technique; no application to grant budgets was
found in this scan.

The lane kills any claim that the *pattern* is new — trestle, Vale, and
docassemble own it. All six claims therefore rest on the grant-domain
objects: menus, fractions, funder packs, statutory rates. That is where the
sweep found no occupants.

## Compensation benchmarking

Does any tool compute loaded personnel costs from rules rather than
multipliers? Benchmarks turn out to be data products, and loading is either
a flat multiplier (grant practice) or a rules-based calculation in payroll
tools that never touch grant budgets and carry no benchmark provenance.

[Candid's Nonprofit Compensation Report](https://candid.org/nonprofit-compensation-report/)
studies executive compensation from IRS 990s — the 2025 edition covers 217k
records across 131k organizations, by position, budget band, and geography —
a benchmark *source*, and a static product.
[ERI's Nonprofit Comparables Assessor](https://www.erieri.com/nonprofitcomparablesassessor)
provides 990-derived comparables for 55 executive positions, supports
rebuttable-presumption-of-reasonableness documentation, and tracks
compensation against department budgets — benchmarks and audit rationale, no
statutory loading. [BLS OEWS](https://www.bls.gov/oes/) publishes wage
percentiles for roughly 830 occupations at national, state, and metro levels
— a provenance substrate C3 can consume; BLS publishes data, not loaded-cost
tooling. A genre of free
[true-cost-of-employee calculators](https://truetools.org/tools/employee-cost-calculator-usa)
computes employer FICA, FUTA, and SUTA from published parameters — some
[citing IRS Publication 15](https://jupid.com/payroll-tax-calculator) — plus
rule-of-thumb benefit and overhead percentages: partial prior art for C3's
computation, as standalone web tools that handle no retirement-plan employer
caps as law, carry no benchmark provenance, and feed no budget artifact.
Grant practice itself budgets personnel as salary times a pooled fringe rate
— the Kuali and Cayuse mechanics above — a configured multiplier.

C3's parts all exist separately: benchmarks in Candid, ERI, and BLS;
rules-based employer-tax calculation in web calculators; and pooled fringe
rates in Kuali and Cayuse. Composing them into a reproducible pre-award rate
artifact capable of carrying optional benchmark provenance is the unoccupied
square.

## Adjacent fields

Beyond the assigned lanes sit the closest conceptual neighbors — the ones a
referee will raise.

Government contracting has long used structured cost buildup.
[Deltek ProPricer](https://www.propricer.com/) — "refined through decades,"
per the vendor — generates "compliant, submission-ready cost volumes" for
CAS-, FAR-, and TINA-governed pricing from labor categories, reusable rate
structures, and overhead and G&A indirects — the strongest C1 neighbor found
in this scan. The differences that keep C1 alive: closed; priced in
labor-category hours, not work items with completion evidence; no
cross-proposal allocation constraint; no CI or reproducibility story; wrap
rates as pooled multipliers (the C3 contrast again).
[BOEMax](https://www.projstream.com/basis-of-estimate-proposal-software-boemax)
reuses historical projects and actuals across proposals — "fast, auditable
reuse," with AI-driven recall of similar past tasks: the
nearest neighbor to C4's menu, with no co-funding fractions (GovCon prices
one contract at a time), no sum-to-one gate, no funder-facing view.

On the philanthropy side, the
[Philanthropy Data Commons](https://philanthropydatacommons.org/) is
shared-data infrastructure — a nonprofit maintains "one verified profile
connecting to any participating funder," exchanged with consent, with
[an API as "the central integration point"](https://philanthropydatacommons.org/howitworks/architecture/)
— C4-adjacent on the *data* axis, but the shared objects are verified org
profiles, not priced work items, with no budget or allocation semantics.
[Common grant applications](https://learning.candid.org/resources/knowledge-base/common-grant-application/)
— regional grantmaker associations, JustFund — are C4's inverse: N funders,
one *form*, no org-side substrate, no fractions.
[Braided-funding practice](https://ecbraiding.mathematica.org/) — the
[HHS/ASPE toolkit](https://www.aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/2021-08/EC_Braiding_Toolkit.pdf)
and Mathematica's early-childhood braiding tool — is C2 and C4's conceptual
ancestor in program finance: each funder pays its share, no double-charging,
enforced by guides, spreadsheets, and humans.

Three funder-facing surfaces frame C6.
[DonorsChoose](https://help.donorschoose.org/hc/en-us/articles/201936606-Prices-in-the-shopping-portal)
prices classroom-project materials through its integrated-vendor shopping
portal, with price deltas reconciled by policy — savings fund additional
projects, cost increases up to 10% absorbed, larger ones resolved by
swapping items within the posted price — the nearest C6 neighbor, but the
items are retail SKUs, not the org's cost model, and there is no
configurator over rates or assumptions.
[Open Collective](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/budget)
keeps collective budgets transparent — "everyone can see where the money
comes from and what it's spent on," per documentation the platform now
banners as out of date — exposing recent transactions, balance, and totals
raised and disbursed on the public page: live *actuals*, not a forward cost
model, with no selection or toggle semantics. [Manifund](https://manifund.org/)
runs public regranting with projects, funding goals, a grant ledger, and
impact-certificate experiments — budgets as prose numbers, not models.

## Adjudication

No lane produced an occupant of the full stack. The adjudication is
summarized in @tbl-verdicts. Two claims lost their loose forms: C1's
"computing budgets from data" is dead (Kuali, Cayuse, ProPricer), and C3's
"computing employer burden from rules" is dead (web calculators); each
survives only as stated — the
pure-function, work-item, CI-reproducible form of C1, and the composed,
pre-award C3 form capable of carrying optional benchmark provenance. C5 is
repositioned rather than defended: its core — machine-encoded funder rules,
automatic validation, a
structured error report — exists at scale in NIH ASSIST, and its pattern —
versioned rule packs validated in CI — exists in compliance-trestle; the
claim is the join, open, applicant-controlled, local, and portable across
funders. C2, C4, and C6 stand as novel in their mechanisms, each with named
ancestors: the NIH overlap rule and effort reporting for C2; BOE reuse, the
APD regime, and data commons for C4; vendor-priced project items and live
ledgers for C6.

| Claim | Verdict | Nearest neighbors |
|---|---|---|
| C1 budget as compiled artifact | Partial prior art | [Kuali Research budget engine](https://kuali-research.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/115010656047-Proposal-Budget-Budget-Engine-Calculations) (rate-table autocalc; open-source ancestor frozen since 2017); [Deltek ProPricer](https://www.propricer.com/) (structured cost buildup) |
| C2 pre-award over-allocation gate | Novel as a machine check; related anti-overlap policy is old | [NIH commitment-overlap rule](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/policy/nihgps/HTML5/section_2/2.5.1_just-in-time_procedures.htm), staff-resolved at award; [Huron ECC](https://finance.uw.edu/pafc/effort-reporting/ecc-system/ecc-overview) post-award reporting |
| C3 rule-derived personnel rates | Partial prior art | [Payroll-tax calculators](https://jupid.com/payroll-tax-calculator) (rules-based loading, no provenance, post-hire); [pooled fringe rates](https://support.cayuse.com/hc/en-us/articles/115013737108-Adding-Fringe-Rates-and-Benefits-in-Proposals-S2S) (the incumbent) |
| C4 funder-as-view | Novel as a mechanism; ancestors reuse estimates or share profiles without fractional constraints | [BOEMax](https://www.projstream.com/basis-of-estimate-proposal-software-boemax) historical-estimate reuse; [Philanthropy Data Commons](https://philanthropydatacommons.org/) (one profile, many funders) |
| C5 versioned funder packs + CI + status artifact | Exists (core, closed); partial (open, applicant-controlled packaging) | [NIH ASSIST](https://www.era.nih.gov/about-era/other-services/validations) business-rule validation; [compliance-trestle](https://github.com/oscal-compass/compliance-trestle) rule packs in git + CI |
| C6 funder-facing configurator | Novel; thinnest neighbor set, adoption untested | [DonorsChoose](https://help.donorschoose.org/hc/en-us/articles/201936606-Prices-in-the-shopping-portal) vendor-priced project items; [Open Collective](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/budget) transparent budget and ledger |

: Claim × verdict × nearest neighbor, from the August 2026 sweep
(2026-08-14/15). {#tbl-verdicts}

Two closing notes. The exact phrases "grants as code" and "CI for grants"
had no prior grant-application use identified in the 2026-08 sweep; the
nearest live practice found was
[crypto grant programs run as markdown pull requests](https://github.com/w3f/Grants-Program).
And the verdicts rest on absence of evidence in a US-centric,
English-language sweep: *novel* means no prior art found, not proven absent.

# The pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

<!-- Reconciled 2026-08-15 through the latest committed state of the 0.3
review branch (grantkit feat/budget-model @ f53da71:
menu/{schema,engine,gates,render,loader}.py,
tests/conftest.py, tests/test_{menu_engine,budget_cli}.py,
docs/budget-model.md) and the reference provider (eggnest-employer
feat/rates-export @ 52a0c6f: rates_export.py, taxes.py, retirement.py,
README, emitted export). Concurrent, uncommitted solver work remained in the
grantkit worktree; re-verify after it lands and before publication. -->

The budget model is implemented on a review branch for the planned grantkit
0.3 release: three YAML document types, a pure-function engine, a set of
gates, and a new CLI verb, `budget`, alongside the existing pack verbs
(`check` and `build` among them). The design keeps a strict engine/data
boundary: 0.3 will ship the schemas and engine, while the review repository
contains synthetic test fixtures; an organization's menus, rates, and
selections live in the organization's own repositories. The budget path is
stateless and local-first — no network calls, no model in the loop — and
compilation is deterministic: saved Markdown and JSON artifacts are
byte-identical for the same inputs. Money is held as floats internally;
human-readable tables and Markdown render whole dollars, while JSON preserves
the numeric values.

## Three documents

**The menu** (`grantkit-menu/v0`) is the organization's priced work-item
catalog. It may carry org-level economics — in v0.3 a single overhead, the
fiscal-sponsorship rate, with optional provenance — and named unit costs,
each a unit price with optional derivation and provenance. Every item has an
id; a type (free vocabulary, with recommended values program-coverage,
platform, research-eval, field, and org-base); a title; a short description
of what it is; a required, non-empty completion-evidence field; a
status (shipped, in-flight, or planned); a dependency list whose ids must
resolve; and a non-empty provenance list. The engine validates the evidence
field for presence; it does not verify completion or enforce that the named
evidence is machine-checkable. An item's resourcing block prices it in any
of five ways, at least one required: FTE-months by role (roles must exist in
the rates file), unit counts (names must exist in the unit costs), flat
contract dollars, recurring dollars per year (prorated over a selection's
window), or a flat amount (the shape org-base blocks use). A flat or
contract amount can declare `overhead_included: true`, meaning the amount
already contains org overheads and the selection-level overhead must not
apply again; the default is false. The v0 schema tolerates unknown extension
keys, so an optional-key typo is ignored rather than guessed: producers must
spell `overhead_included` exactly or its false default remains in effect. The
flag exists because upstream org models emit fee-inclusive totals —
@sec-case shows what happens without it.

**The rates file** (`grantkit-rates/v0`) is designed as a contract with a
rates provider, although the schema cannot prevent hand-entered values. It
must carry a non-empty provider identifier — conventionally a name and
version — plus its generation date and currency, and may carry a scenario
id, jurisdiction, and prose method. Each role carries a required annual
`loaded_usd`, a recommended base, an optional SOC code, an optional component
breakdown, and an optional benchmark. Every component states its basis from
a closed vocabulary — computed (derived from encoded rules or data),
configured (a scenario input someone chose), or assumed (a placeholder) —
plus an optional source string. Benchmark source, percentile, and dollar
value are each optional. The reference provider normally supplies all three
and adds the organization's computed market percentile as a provider-specific
extra; grantkit tolerates but does not render that extra. grantkit validates
the rates document against its schema; it does not recompute a provider's
law-based numbers — that is the provider's job, under the provider's tests.

The reference provider, eggnest-employer, defines a role's `loaded_usd` as
modeled guaranteed employer cost: base salary, plus employer retirement,
plus configured other compensation, plus employer payroll taxes when an
employer tax state is configured. The taxes are computed from encoded rules
via policyengine-us — Social Security and Medicare, plus unemployment and
local payroll taxes when the installed variables are available. Bonus and
equity are excluded from the guaranteed package, and health and other
benefits are not modeled; every export's method paragraph states those
exclusions. Two implementation caveats matter when interpreting the optional
tax figures.
State unemployment uses an encoded model default — a statewide new-employer
rate where available, otherwise a reported average — and is therefore not
necessarily the organization's experience rate. When aggregate-local mode is
configured, the provider computes scenario-level local payroll tax, including
New York MCTMT, on aggregate organizational payroll through the encoded
bracket schedules. It then uses a payroll-tax-gross-wage-weighted adjustment
to reconcile the per-role local estimates to that total, so the resulting
per-role local-tax figures are allocations rather than per-role legal
calculations. When the scenario selects the statutory cap
source, the provider constructs an employer retirement ceiling as the IRS
415(c) annual-additions limit minus the 402(g) elective limit, both resolved
from policyengine-us parameters. It states this as a conservative modeling
assumption, because the identity assumes the employee defers the full
elective limit, and labels that component basis-computed; a scenario-fixed
amount or cap is basis-configured. If an employer tax state is absent, or if
an installed PolicyEngine-US build lacks optional employer-side variables,
the provider records the omission in the role or method and, for the
variable fallback, emits a `RuntimeWarning`; degradation never passes
silently.

Two advisory warnings police the seam for roles with a positive base. A
load-factor check flags any role whose loaded-to-base ratio falls below 1.05
("loaded is barely above base (pasted base as loaded?)") or above 2.0 — a
bug class observed in the wild, when three roles in a seeded menu carried
base salary pasted as loaded cost. When a component breakdown is present, a
components check flags any breakdown that misses the stated loaded cost by
more than a dollar.

**A selection** (`grantkit-selection/v0`) is a proposal: an id, a funder, a
status from a closed vocabulary (draft, live, awarded, withdrawn, declined),
an optional advisory target, a required window in months, an optional
org-base allocation (an item that must be of type org-base, with a fraction
between zero and one), and an ordered list of selected items, each with a
co-funding fraction. Explicit zero fractions are preserved and meaningful:
an item selected at fraction 0.0 — optionally with a note — is *declared,
not allocated here*: the funder sees that the work exists in the plan and
that this proposal pays none of it.

A portfolio directory holds the menu, the rates file, and a `selections/`
directory of proposals (a single selection file beside the menu also works
for one-proposal setups). A grant project can bind itself to one selection
through its `grant.yaml`, pointing at the portfolio and naming the
selection.

## The engine

Compilation is two pure functions. Item cost: labor is the sum over roles of
FTE-months divided by twelve times the role's loaded annual cost; units are
count times unit price; contract and flat amounts pass through; these sum to
a one-time cost, with recurring dollars carried separately. Selection cost:
each selected item contributes its fraction times its one-time cost, plus
its fraction times its recurring cost prorated by the window (months over
twelve); the org base contributes its fraction times the org-base item's
one-time cost, deliberately not window-prorated — flat blocks are priced as
blocks, matching upstream practice; overhead applies the org's rate to every
component except those whose amount came from a field flagged
`overhead_included`, which makes the fee idempotent by construction; the
total is work plus base plus overhead, and when the selection declares a
positive target, the compilation reports fit as total over target.

## The gates

`grantkit budget --check` runs the integrity gates over a whole portfolio
and exits nonzero on errors: 1 when error findings are reported, and 2 when the
command's usage, project binding, portfolio, or requested selection cannot be
resolved. The integrity errors include schema violations in any of the three
documents; a mismatch
between the menu and rates currencies; duplicate selection ids; references
that do not resolve — a selection naming a missing item, an item
naming a missing role or unit, a dependency naming a missing item;
dependency cycles, found by depth-first search in deterministic order;
fractions outside zero to one; an org-base reference to an item that is not
of type org-base; the same item listed twice in one selection's ordered item
list; and the C2 gate, `cofunding_over_allocated`, which for every item sums
fractions across all selections with status live or awarded and fails if the sum
exceeds one (with a 1e-9 tolerance), naming each contributing selection and
its fraction in the message. Org-base fractions count toward the same
per-item sums, labeled as org-base contributions in the finding. Draft,
withdrawn, and declined selections are excluded
by design: drafts are free to over-plan, and the gate fires when they enter
live status. In v0.3, status is the concurrency proxy: the gate
conservatively treats every live or awarded selection as overlapping because
the schema carries a window length but no start date, end date, or completed
status. It does not infer temporal overlap.

The warnings: a selected work item depends on work that is neither shipped,
in-flight, funded in any live or awarded selection, nor funded by the
selection itself — the proposal assumes work nobody has funded; the
compiled total exceeds a positive declared target (advisory — a target is an
ask, not a cap); and the rates-contract heuristics above. Inside a grant
project bound to a selection, if the funder pack declares a total or annual
cap, a currency mismatch is an error because grantkit does not convert
currencies. When currencies match, the pack's total cap applies to the
compiled total as an error, reusing the existing cap identifier; the annual
cap — approximated as total times twelve over the window months, a
uniform-spread approximation — is checked as a warning.

## The budget verb

`grantkit budget` prints the compilation as tables: per-item costs,
per-role personnel, and a category summary. `--json` emits the full
structured compilation. `--output` writes a markdown budget document: a
header stating the selection, funder, window, and status; a generated-from
line reporting the menu schema and currency and the rates-provider
identifier and generation date, plus a scenario when present; a
selected-items table with fractions, item costs, and funded shares; a
personnel table with fraction-weighted FTE-months, loaded annual rates, and a
benchmark column when at least one selected role has a benchmark source; and
a category summary showing the nonzero categories drawn from labor, units,
contract, flat, recurring prorated, org base, and overhead, followed by the
total and a target-fit line when the target is positive. The generated-from
line is provenance metadata, not an input hash. `--narrative` appends a
narrative skeleton: for each funded item, its title, what it is, its
completion evidence, and its cost line; then a budget-justification
skeleton per role, with a benchmark-provenance sentence where present. The
narrative renders from the compiled objects only — no generated prose
beyond connective boilerplate.

## Continuous integration

When CI is configured, a portfolio repository runs `grantkit budget --check`;
a grant project bound to a selection through `grant.yaml` can also run
`grantkit check`, which folds the selection gates and funder caps into the
pack-check findings stream and exit-code semantics. A broken invariant then
fails the CI check just as a missing required section does. When an output is
regenerated, a changed rate or fraction used by that selection produces a
narrow derived-table diff. `--check` does not itself compare a saved output,
so CI that requires artifact freshness needs a separate regeneration-and-diff
step. The C2 rule re-verifies on every schema-valid portfolio check, including
checks after edits to other proposals, because it binds the loaded portfolio
rather than only the file being edited. A regenerated artifact can be shared
with the funder from the same inputs the organization uses for planning.

The review repository's test suite compiles a synthetic portfolio — three
roles (one with a full component breakdown and benchmark, one base-only, one
loaded-only), six items (including a fee-inclusive org-base block, units,
recurring cost, a dependency chain, and shipped work), and three selections
(two live selections sharing an item at 0.5 each, and a draft over-planner
carrying an explicit-zero declaration). The tests assert the arithmetic and
byte-identical Markdown from repeated runs. For a one-selection reproduction,
the following category summary was generated directly by the 0.3 review
branch's `budget` verb from those synthetic input shapes:

# Case study {#sec-case}

<!-- Reconcile pass: every figure in this section re-verifies against the
gated diligence model (private org repo) before publication. -->

The pipeline's first run on organization data was an August 2026
diligence sprint at The Axiom Foundation, presented here with funders
unnamed. The substrate was one configured rates file plus a menu of 25 priced
items — 22 work items and three fee-inclusive org-base blocks — seeded from
the sprint's diligence corpus. The rates were planning figures pending
replacement by a reference-provider export, so this case does not demonstrate
C3's rule-derived computation. Figures are from the sprint's working records.

During the sprint, a bottoms-up org model derived four org shapes — $21.2
million to $37.8 million over five years — from shared role rates and
documented unit costs. Each shape is a configuration of the same model, so a
changed rate or assumption regenerates all four together; fee-inclusive
org-cost blocks from that model became the menu's org-base items, which
selections claim fractionally. The ad-hoc pricer's first pass on a $2 million
concept note printed 134% of target; the typed compilation printed
$2,578,998.57, or 129.0% — exposing a $99,750 fee double-application, about
five percentage points, and a real roughly 29-point overshoot, both before
submission. The remaining scope is a trim decision in the organization's
repository. The model also represented the bottom and top of a three-level
funder structure as distinct selections over the same menu, with different
item sets and org-base blocks.

The compilation also exposed an unresolved pricing decision recorded in the
source model: a levy versus a full-price posture for attestation. Pricing the
menu represented that decision as an explicit organizational choice rather
than leaving it implicit in a budget total.

One discovery is worth stating mechanically, because it is the shape of
error this compilation catches. An upstream org-cost block already carried
a 7% fiscal-sponsorship fee inside its total. An ad-hoc pricer multiplied
that block by 1.07 again. In the typed substrate, the block is a flat amount
with the recognized field `overhead_included: true`, so the engine exempts it
from selection-level overhead and the fee applies exactly once for that
input.
Porting the model removed the $99,750 phantom from the concept-note view and
moved it from 134% to 129% of its target. The remaining overshoot was priced
scope, not the duplicated fee — a distinction the ad-hoc pricer had obscured.

# What this does not solve {#sec-limits}

The pipeline does not write the proposal. Narrative quality and relationship
work are untouched; the system establishes numbers consistent with the
declared inputs and model, not their truth, completeness, reasonableness, or
external billing. The menu, rates, and fractions can be wrong or incomplete,
and the completion-evidence field is required data rather than a verification
of completed work. Formula spreadsheets can also implement deterministic
arithmetic; the claimed advantage here is inspectable schema/data separation,
textual diffs, headless checks, and portfolio-wide constraints.

The over-allocation gate sees only selections loaded in one portfolio and
trusts their item identities, fractions, and statuses. It cannot detect an
omitted off-repository proposal or two semantically duplicate items with
different ids. It also treats every live and awarded selection as
simultaneous: v0.3 has a window length but no calendar dates or completed
award status. Marking a proposal live before sending it is a workflow
convention, not an enforced submission integration.

Funder adoption of configurators is untested; the diligence in @sec-case
pressure-tested scenarios by recompiling the model, without a funder-facing
interface. The case used configured planning rates rather than a
reference-provider export. That provider covers federal and supported
state/local employer-payroll rules when configured, plus the stated
retirement-cap scenario; omissions are recorded, and the optional-variable
fallback also emits a warning. Funder packs likewise depend on maintainers to
keep rules current, and an authoritative submission portal remains the final
check. Mechanically,
v0.3 prorates recurring costs over a single window — no multi-year phasing —
and assumes single-currency portfolios.

The novelty is also bounded as adjudicated in @sec-landscape: budget
compilation and rule-derived rates are partially anticipated by rate-table
engines and payroll calculators, while the core of automated funder-rule
validation already runs at scale, closed, in NIH ASSIST. The claims are the
precise C1 and C3 compositions, the C2 and C4 mechanisms, the proposed C6
surface, and C5's open, applicant-controlled packaging — not those looser
forms.

# Discussion and conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

The landscape scan narrows the contribution more than it expands it. C1 and
C3 retain only their precise, composed forms; C5 retains an open,
local, funder-portable packaging around a validation core that already
exists; and C2, C4, and C6 are absence-of-prior-art findings under the scan's
stated scope. The implemented review branch demonstrates compilation,
portfolio selections, and the status-based allocation gate. It does not yet
demonstrate a released 0.3 package, public end-to-end reference-rate
generation, a funder-facing configurator, or organizational use beyond one
private case.

In that case, typed compilation separated a $99,750 duplicated fee from the
remaining priced scope and made a pricing-policy choice explicit. That is
evidence of one detected arithmetic error, not an estimate of general error
rates or effectiveness. The narrower thesis survives: versioned inputs,
deterministic compilation, and explicit checks can make proposal budgets
reproducible and reviewable before submission. Whether organizations and
funders adopt the workflow, and whether it improves outcomes, remain
empirical questions.

# Availability {#sec-availability}

<!-- PUBLICATION GATE (2026-08-15): release grantkit 0.3 to PyPI before

Organization data repositories remain private. The synthetic fixture lives
in the review repository's tests, not in the current 0.2.x wheel; do not call
it packaged unless 0.3 packaging changes. -->

grantkit 0.2.x is available on PyPI today under the MIT license. The menu,
rates, and selection schemas and the budget engine described here are
implemented on the review branch for the companion 0.3 release; they are not
in the current PyPI release. The review repository's test suite contains the
synthetic fixture used above, but the current 0.2.x PyPI distribution does not
ship that fixture. The reference rates provider, eggnest-employer, is not yet
public; its release is pending. Organization menus and selections remain in
private organization repositories. The case-study figures in @sec-case come
from those records; the synthetic compilation demonstrates the engine path
without reproducing the private provider or case data.
